strengths: Significance: Learning feasible link topologies for directional-antenna ad hoc networks is a useful application. Conditioning generation on node positions and orientations, while incorporating antenna-sector and parity constraints, provides a coherent problem-specific approach.

Originality: Cross-Attentive Modulation (CAM) offers a potentially useful architectural extension: learned tokens aggregate graph information and condition feature modulation on interactions with individual nodes. Combining this mechanism with topology-specific losses is a discernible contribution, although its advantage over existing global-conditioning mechanisms needs stronger validation.

Empirical merits: Tables 1–3 show consistent improvements over the reported graph-transformer baseline. Connected graphs increase from 98.12% to 99.13%, saturated antennas decrease from 24.59% to 16.19%, and simulated throughput increases from 1.49 to 1.60 Mbps. The loss ablation also suggests that explicit parity supervision substantially improves constraint adherence.

Presentation and limitations: The manuscript has an understandable overall organization and useful architectural illustrations. It acknowledges residual constraint violations, the need for post-processing, and the lack of a substantial 32-node evaluation. No material research-ethics concern is apparent in the described synthetic-network experiments.
weaknesses: Soundness—operational feasibility is not established. Interference avoidance motivates the problem, but the paper provides neither a sufficiently specified interference model nor direct interference-violation measurements. Algorithm 2 removes redundant sector links and reconnects components without explicitly checking parity, maximum range, or interference; it also lacks a failure condition when no feasible reconnection exists. No post-repair constraint-adherence or throughput results demonstrate that the resulting networks are operational. High marginal compliance rates before repair do not establish simultaneous feasibility.

Soundness—the temporal contribution is unsupported experimentally. Section 4.3 proposes partial diffusion for moving nodes, but reports no mobility experiments, topology-change rates, connectivity over time, or throughput under movement. The assertion that a previous topology does not inherently differ from a noisy training graph because their edge marginals agree is unjustified: matching marginals does not establish matching joint or position-conditioned distributions. The conclusion's claim of a robust mobility mechanism therefore exceeds the evidence.

Significance and efficiency—the evaluation does not establish an advantage over practical topology construction. The only learned comparator is a standard graph transformer; there is no measured runtime/quality comparison against the greedy data generator or another topology heuristic. Reported inference takes approximately 480 ms on GPU or 2 seconds on CPU, with repair taking up to 250 ms, but these figures alone do not demonstrate acceleration. The scalability argument omits the full cost of 50 diffusion steps through 10 transformer blocks and relies on an unspecified relationship between candidate-link count and node count. Quantitative evaluation is limited to 16-node graphs.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript omits exact dataset sizes and splits, the position/orientation distributions, deployment geometry and range parameters, the interference threshold and complete data-generation procedure, and the throughput simulator's traffic and routing assumptions. Model widths, attention-head and CAM-token counts, loss weights, training duration, batch size, and the actual learning-rate schedule are also unspecified. Section 4.3 additionally omits the movement thresholds and mappings to diffusion steps and guidance strength. No code or dataset availability information resolves these omissions.

Methodological specification contains consequential ambiguities. Equation (4), described as standard cross-attention, omits softmax, although Figure 2 includes it. The scalar transition-matrix description and Equation (1) do not clearly specify a normalized categorical reverse kernel or the marginalization over clean edge states. The paper also does not explain how the neighbor-set-dependent cosine loss is differentiated through predicted links or handled for nodes with fewer than two neighbors. These issues leave the implemented method uncertain.

Originality and attribution are insufficiently isolated. CAM is related to the global FiLM conditioning and register mechanisms already discussed in the paper, but there is no direct comparison with these alternatives or a parameter-matched control. Tables 1–3 provide some component evidence, yet do not clearly establish which losses and features are shared across all architectural variants, nor separate the cosine and sector penalties. Consequently, the improvements cannot confidently be attributed to the proposed global-control mechanism.

Presentation and evidential precision need improvement. Section 5.1 defines Parity as the proportion of links that violate parity, while the tables mark larger values as better and the discussion treats 98.65% as successful adherence. Exact test counts, repeated-run variability, and confidence intervals are absent, making small differences difficult to assess. The acknowledged limitations are appropriate, but the conclusion still makes broader claims of efficiency, scalability, and operational reliability than the experiments support.

strengths: Significance: Learning feasible directional-antenna network topologies is a useful application of conditional graph generation. The combination of connectivity, antenna-sector capacity, parity, and mobility provides a meaningful engineering problem.

Empirical merits: NetDiff improves over the reported graph-transformer baseline. Connected graphs increase from 98.12% to 99.13%, saturated nodes decrease from 17.08% to 12.31%, and simulated throughput increases from 1.49 to 1.60 Mbps (Tables 1–2). Table 3 also provides evidence that the auxiliary losses improve constraint adherence.

Originality: Cross-attentive modulation offers a plausible architectural extension that combines learned global aggregation with node-dependent feature modulation. Its application to this constrained topology-generation task has potential.

Presentation and limitations: The manuscript has an accessible overall structure and explicitly acknowledges residual violations, the need for post-processing, and the lack of a full 32-node evaluation. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the described synthetic-network experiments.
weaknesses: Soundness—operational feasibility is not established. Interference avoidance motivates the entire task, but the paper provides neither a reproducible interference model nor direct interference-violation measurements. Algorithm 2 repairs sector redundancy and connectivity without explicitly checking parity, maximum range, or interference when adding links. It also lacks a failure condition when no feasible component-connecting link exists. No post-repair feasibility or throughput results support the claim that the generated networks become operational after minor corrections.

Soundness—network evolution is essentially unvalidated. Section 4.3 proposes partial diffusion and guidance, but reports no mobility experiments, link-turnover measurements, temporal connectivity, or comparison with regeneration and simple local repair. Matching edge marginals does not establish that a previous topology under changed coordinates follows the training corruption distribution. Consequently, the claim that this procedure maintains performance and stable configurations is unsupported.

Significance—efficiency and scalability claims exceed the evidence. The reported 480 ms GPU inference, approximately 2 s CPU inference, and up to 250 ms repair time are not compared with the greedy generator or other topology algorithms. A per-layer quadratic complexity argument does not establish an end-to-end advantage for a 50-step, 10-block diffusion model. Quantitative evaluation is confined to 16 nodes; the informal observation about 32 nodes cannot substantiate scalability.

Evaluation and originality: Comparisons are largely restricted to a standard graph-transformer DDPM. There is no measured quality–runtime comparison with conventional topology construction, the cited wireless diffusion approach, or simpler learned alternatives. CAM is not compared with matched-capacity global pooling, virtual tokens, or existing graph-level FiLM conditioning. Tables 1–3 provide useful partial ablations, but no seeds, uncertainty estimates, or sufficiently explicit configuration details to establish how robustly the proposed mechanism explains the gains.

Reproducibility: Essential details are absent, including exact dataset sizes and coordinate distributions, the teacher's interference threshold and complete selection procedure, parity-label construction, the throughput simulator and traffic/routing assumptions, model widths and attention heads, loss weights, training duration, and the movement-to-diffusion/guidance schedules. Reporting AdamW and a learning-rate range is insufficient to reproduce the results; no code or dataset availability statement is provided.

Methodological specification and presentation: Equation 4 omits the softmax required by the stated standard attention, although Figure 2 includes it. The binary diffusion transition is described as a scalar without fully defining its categorical interpretation, and the sampling equations omit the explicit marginalization over clean edge states. Equation 11 depends on discrete neighbor sets without explaining differentiation through predicted edges or handling nodes with fewer than two neighbors. These ambiguities leave consequential implementation choices unresolved.

Interpretation of results: Table 1 defines Parity as the fraction of violating links while marking higher values as better and interpreting 98.65% as adherence. This needs correction. More broadly, Table 2 still shows substantially more saturated antennas than the target graphs (16.19% versus 9.74%), longer links (1.04 versus 0.85), and lower throughput (1.60 versus 1.72 Mbps). The acknowledged limitations are appropriate, but the conclusion's claims of robust mobility handling and an operational, scalable solution are not supported by the experiments. These central evidential and reproducibility gaps warrant rejection despite the promising static results.

strengths: Significance: Generating directional wireless network topologies under geometric and connectivity constraints is a useful application. Conditioning graph diffusion on node positions and orientations is a plausible approach to learning from expensive topology construction procedures.

Empirical merits: NetDiff improves over the reported graph-transformer baseline: connected graphs increase from 98.12% to 99.13%, saturated antennas decrease from 24.59% to 16.19%, and simulated user throughput increases from 1.49 to 1.60 Mbps (Tables 1–2). Table 3 also provides useful evidence that the additional losses improve constraint adherence.

Originality: Cross-attentive modulation offers a potentially useful combination of learned global aggregation and node-dependent feature modulation. Reusing previous topologies during partial diffusion is also a sensible proposal for reducing network reconfiguration.

Presentation and limitations: The overall pipeline is understandable, with architecture illustrations and explicit repair pseudocode. The authors acknowledge residual constraint violations and the absence of comprehensive 32-node evaluation. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the described work.
weaknesses: Soundness—operational validity is not established. Interference avoidance motivates the work, but the experiments provide no explicit interference metric or sufficiently specified interference model. Table 2 reports 16.19% saturated antennas, and Table 1 still shows range and parity violations under the apparent intended interpretation. Algorithm 2 does not explicitly check interference, parity, or maximum range when adding links, and its reconnection loop has no stated fallback when feasible links are unavailable. No post-repair validity or throughput results substantiate the claim that the output becomes operational after minor corrections.

Soundness—the mobility contribution is unevaluated. Section 4.3 proposes topology reuse and movement-dependent diffusion, but reports no moving-node experiments, link-change rates, connectivity over time, or comparison with regeneration and simple local repair. Matching marginal edge frequencies does not establish that a previous topology under changed geometry follows the training corruption distribution. The conclusion's claim of robust operation under mobility therefore exceeds the evidence.

Significance and efficiency: Quantitative evaluation is limited to 16-node synthetic networks. There is no measured comparison against the greedy data generator, a conventional topology heuristic, or other relevant learned methods. The reported 480 ms GPU inference and up to 250 ms repair do not establish a speed advantage without corresponding baseline timings. The scalability argument also needs to account for 50 diffusion steps, graph density, and repair costs; anecdotal observations on 32 nodes are insufficient.

Reproducibility: Essential details are missing, including dataset sizes and spatial distributions, the precise topology-generation heuristic and interference threshold, communication and throughput simulation assumptions, architecture widths and CAM configuration, loss weights, training duration, and movement-to-diffusion mappings. Reporting AdamW and a learning-rate range does not define a reproducible training procedure. No code or dataset availability statement is provided.

Technical specification and presentation: Equation (4) omits the softmax used in standard attention and shown in Figure 2. The binary diffusion transition is described as a scalar without clearly specifying the transition kernel, and Equation (1) leaves the clean-edge marginalization unclear. Equation (11) does not explain differentiability through predicted neighborhoods or handling of nodes with fewer than two neighbors. The text defines 'Parity' as the fraction of violating links, whereas the tables and discussion treat larger values as better. These ambiguities affect implementation and interpretation.

Originality and attribution: CAM builds on established attention pooling, global tokens, and FiLM modulation, but is not compared with simpler pooled global conditioning or register-token alternatives. The limited ablations do not isolate the individual loss contributions or establish which CAM design choices matter. Claims about improved global reasoning and reduced oversmoothing lack direct analysis. Exact test counts, repeated-run variability, and uncertainty estimates are also absent. The promising static results do not outweigh the unresolved validation and reproducibility gaps.

strengths: Significance: Jointly generating directional links and two-slot transmit/receive parity addresses a useful, practically motivated problem. Learning from expensive topology optimization and updating existing solutions under mobility are sensible approaches.

Originality: ACAM combines unnormalized, permutation-invariant cross-attention aggregation with FiLM modulation. Its ability to preserve information about aggregate magnitude provides a plausible mechanism for improving sector occupancy predictions.

Empirical merits: Table 1 reports improved link throughput and reduced antenna saturation over DDPM-GT, including its feature-enhanced variant. Table 2 reports 78.92 Mbps versus 75.43 for DDPM-GT and 79.33 for the reference on 16-node networks. The loss ablation also shows substantial improvements in parity compliance.

Presentation and ethics: The paper is generally readable, illustrates the architecture and update procedures, and provides training settings and correction pseudocode. It acknowledges the proprietary simulator, the need for mixed-size training, and deployment risks. No material ethical violation is evident.
weaknesses: Reproducibility: Central experimental components are unavailable or insufficiently specified. Appendix 8 explicitly omits the physical simulation parameters, while throughput depends on proprietary propagation models and an unspecified power-control module. Appendix 7 describes the primary quasi-exhaustive solver only qualitatively, without its search procedure, budget, or fallback frequency. The main dataset size, layout distribution, train/validation/test splits, and test sample counts are missing. These omissions prevent independent verification of the headline performance.

Soundness of feasibility claims: Raw predictions retain constraint violations, and the correction procedure does not guarantee the claimed valid, connected output. Algorithm 2 explicitly permits termination with disconnected components. Its edge-addition step checks interference on the candidate link but does not explicitly recheck interference induced on existing links. Post-correction connectivity, sector compliance, parity compliance, and failure rates are not reported, although throughput measurements use post-processing.

Evaluation and attribution: It is unclear whether every baseline receives identical correction and computational budgets, making the throughput gains difficult to attribute to the learned architecture. Section 5.1 says all models use the additional features and losses, yet Table 1 distinguishes DDPM-GT from DDPM-GT with features. Error bars are undefined, only one training seed is specified, and throughput results lack uncertainty estimates. Matching a heuristic-assisted reference also does not establish proximity to an optimum.

Soundness and specification of diffusion: Equations (4) and (6) do not specify normalized reverse transition distributions or the marginalization over predicted clean states required by the referenced discrete diffusion formulation. The partial-diffusion transition matrices mix identity matrices with previous graph states without explaining their categorical construction. The displacement-to-timestep mapping, guidance coefficients, and auxiliary-loss weights are also unspecified. These are consequential ambiguities for reproducing the proposed method.

Mobility evidence: Section 5.2 starts from reference topologies and evaluates perturbed layouts, rather than repeated updates from the model's own outputs. Continuity is not formally defined, and the reported 21% and 41% similarity improvements lack an explicit paired baseline table or uncertainty estimates. There is no comparison against retaining and repairing the previous topology or an equal-budget shortened full-generation process. Consequently, sustained mobile-network performance and the benefit specific to partial diffusion remain unestablished.

Originality and significance of global capabilities: ACAM is a plausible architectural contribution, but the experiments do not isolate counting ability from added parameters or compare against simple sum-pooling plus FiLM and matched virtual-token alternatives. Connectivity and parity barely change between CAM and ACAM in Table 3. The 32-node experiment requires retraining, so it does not demonstrate size extrapolation. The broader claims about improved global capabilities exceed the evidence.

Runtime claims: A fixed number of diffusion steps does not imply constant runtime with graph size; the transformer processes pairwise graph information, and correction has input-dependent runtime. The reported approximately 450 ms GPU generation time and correction time below 100 ms are useful measurements, but no size-dependent latency study or application-specific deadline establishes the claimed real-time regime.

strengths: Significance: Joint topology and transmit/receive parity generation addresses a useful, practically motivated problem. Learning to approximate expensive topology construction and updating previous solutions under mobility are worthwhile objectives.

Originality: ACAM combines unnormalized cross-attention aggregation with FiLM modulation to provide permutation-invariant global information. Although its components are familiar, their integration offers a plausible mechanism for improving graph-level counting and constraint satisfaction.

Empirical merits: The architectural comparisons provide encouraging evidence. In Table 1, ACAM improves link throughput from 3.35 for DDPM-GT with features to 3.52 and reduces antenna saturation from 13.6% to 12.1%. Table 4 also demonstrates the usefulness of the additional constraint losses.

Presentation and ethics: The overall pipeline is understandable, and the manuscript explicitly acknowledges the throughput proxy, the need for training on larger graphs, and proprietary simulator restrictions. The impact statement identifies plausible misuse and deployment risks; I see no material research-ethics concern established by the manuscript.
weaknesses: Soundness—feasibility is not established for the final system. Raw outputs retain constraint violations, while throughput is measured after correction and other metrics are measured before correction (Section 5.1). Algorithm 2 explicitly allows disconnected outputs when no admissible connecting edge exists. Moreover, its insertion test checks interference for the new link without explicitly rechecking the interference induced on existing links. Thus, the stated enforcement of hard constraints and restoration of connectivity are not guaranteed. Report joint feasibility, throughput changes, and failure rates after correction.

Reproducibility—essential data and evaluation details are missing. Appendix 7 describes the principal quasi-exhaustive solver only qualitatively, without its search procedure, budget, stopping criterion, or fallback frequency. The main dataset size, sampling distribution, train/validation/test split, and evaluation sample counts are unspecified. Appendix 8 explicitly omits simulator parameters and relies on an unspecified external power-control module. Consequently, neither the reference targets nor the central throughput comparisons can be independently reconstructed.

Soundness and presentation—the mathematical specification needs correction. Equation 4 multiplies clean-state predictions by transition terms without specifying the normalized reverse posterior or marginalization over clean states required by discrete diffusion; Equation 6 inherits this ambiguity. Equation 15 weights the angle at node h by the edge between its neighbors i and j, rather than the incident edges defining that angle. In a valid bipartite graph, those neighbors cannot themselves be connected, making the written loss particularly questionable. Its treatment of nodes with fewer than two neighbors is also unspecified. These issues prevent reliable implementation of the stated method.

Evaluation—the evidence does not cleanly isolate the architectural contribution. Section 5.1 says all models use the additional features and losses, yet Table 1 distinguishes DDPM-GT from DDPM-GT with features. Parameter-matched comparisons against virtual tokens or simple sum-pooling followed by FiLM are absent, and the closely related TopoFormer is discussed but not evaluated. Only one training seed is specified, and the meaning of the reported error bars is unexplained. Connectivity and parity differences in Table 3 are especially small relative to those reported uncertainties.

Dynamic-update claims are insufficiently validated. Section 5.2 starts from reference topologies and perturbs coordinates, rather than evaluating repeated updates from the model's own outputs over trajectories. The continuity metric, displacement-to-timestep mapping, and guidance coefficients are not specified sufficiently. Tables 5–6 omit matched full-generation and simple repair baselines on the same moved layouts. Reduced step counts support potential acceleration, but do not establish robustness to accumulated errors or the claimed best accuracy–computation tradeoff.

Significance and claim calibration: Table 2 evaluates an instantaneous throughput upper-bound proxy, not delivered end-to-end network performance or proximity to a certified optimum. The reference itself mixes search and heuristic solutions. Likewise, a fixed number of diffusion steps does not imply constant runtime across graph sizes, and correction has input-dependent cost. The reported approximately 450 ms GPU generation time needs an application-specific deadline and complete pipeline timing to substantiate real-time operation.

Originality and generality remain limited by the evidence. The claimed improvement in global capabilities is supported primarily by aggregate metrics on one specialized setting, without direct counting diagnostics or broader graph benchmarks. Appendix 9 requires retraining with 32-node examples, so it does not establish extrapolation to unseen sizes. These limitations would be acceptable for a carefully validated application contribution, but the unresolved feasibility, specification, and reproducibility gaps currently prevent acceptance.

strengths: Significance: Jointly generating directional links and transmit/receive parity addresses a useful, practically motivated problem with interacting connectivity, interference, and sector constraints. Updating existing topologies through partial diffusion is also operationally relevant.

Originality: ACAM combines unnormalized cross-attention aggregation with global FiLM modulation, providing a plausible mechanism for retaining cardinality information. Its integration into node-conditioned graph diffusion is a meaningful architectural contribution.

Empirical merits: Table 1 shows consistent improvements from domain features, CAM, and ACAM. ACAM improves link throughput from 3.35 to 3.52 over the feature-enhanced diffusion baseline and reduces antenna saturation from 13.6% to 12.1%. Table 4 also supports the usefulness of the constraint losses.

Presentation and ethics: The main architecture and application are reasonably clearly explained. The paper explicitly identifies throughput as an upper-bound proxy, acknowledges the need for training on larger graphs, and discusses misuse and deployment-validation risks. No material ethical violation is apparent.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is insufficient for the central performance claims. Appendix 8 explicitly omits proprietary simulation parameters, while Appendix 7 does not specify the primary search algorithm, search budget, or fallback frequency. Main-dataset sizes, train/validation/test splits, loss weights, and the meaning of reported error bars are also missing. Consequently, neither the supervision nor the throughput evaluation can be reliably reconstructed.

Soundness of feasibility claims: Raw outputs still violate constraints, and the correction algorithm does not guarantee the claimed valid, connected networks. Algorithm 2 explicitly permits termination with disconnected components; adding a link also does not explicitly recheck interference admissibility for existing links. Post-correction connectivity, constraint violations, and repair frequency are not reported. Moreover, the target graphs themselves have 9.7% antenna saturation despite being described as constraint-compliant.

The throughput evidence does not isolate the learned contribution sufficiently. Throughput measurements use post-processing, whereas most other metrics use raw predictions; before/after repair results and a clearly identical repair protocol across baselines are absent. Table 2 is encouraging, but without these controls and uncertainty estimates it cannot establish how much improvement comes from ACAM rather than correction. Matching a reference solver also does not establish near-optimality.

The mobility evaluation is incomplete. Section 5.2 starts from reference topologies and applies coordinate perturbations, without evaluating repeated updates from the model's own outputs. Continuity is not formally defined, the claimed correspondence between motion-induced changes and diffusion states is not measured, and there is no controlled comparison with full regeneration or simple topology repair on the same moved layouts. The reported step-count reduction therefore provides limited evidence for robust deployment under sustained mobility.

Methodological specification contains consequential ambiguities. Equations (4) and (6) multiply clean-state predictions by reverse transition terms without specifying normalization or the marginalization over clean states used in standard discrete diffusion. The modified transition matrices and guidance implementation for partial diffusion are likewise underspecified. These issues prevent confidently determining whether the implemented sampler matches the stated method.

The broader architectural and efficiency claims exceed the evidence. There are no matched-capacity comparisons against simple sum pooling or conventional virtual tokens, nor direct cardinality-prediction experiments, to establish ACAM's distinctive global capabilities. Evaluation is largely limited to 16 nodes, with a separately retrained 32-node model. A fixed number of diffusion steps does not imply constant runtime with graph size, and the reported 450 ms GPU inference time lacks an end-to-end latency comparison against the reference solver and mobility requirements.
